title: Exceptions and Reading Text
lede: Handle expected failures on purpose, follow exceptions through method calls, and read tokens or lines without losing data. Then read real files in Java and Python.

sections.title: Expected failures and specific handlers
concepts: A failure changes control flow

An exception is an object that reports a failure while the program runs, such as bad input or a missing file.

When an operation fails, it throws (Java) or raises (Python) an exception. The rest of the try block is skipped, and the first matching handler runs. Then the program continues after the whole try statement.

With no matching handler, the program stops and prints a report. Java names the exception first. Python names it last, so read a traceback from the bottom up.

Java, no handler
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "bad"
	at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:527)
	...
	at Demo.main(Demo.java:4)
Python, no handler
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "demo.py", line 1, in <module>
    print(int("bad") + 1)
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'bad'
A compile error is not an exception

A Java compile error or a Python SyntaxError stops the program before it runs, so no try can catch it.
Catch what you can explain

Catch only failures you can explain: NumberFormatException around Integer.parseInt, ValueError around int(). Then your message can be exact: Invalid: bad.

Keep the try block small. Otherwise a failure from another line reaches the handler and gets the wrong message. Python’s else runs only if the try succeeded, and the handlers do not cover it.

The empty catch

catch (Exception e) { } and except: pass hide every failure, bugs included. The program goes wrong later, far from the cause. If you catch, do something visible: print a message, use a stated default, or ask again.

Errors should never pass silently.
Unless explicitly silenced.

Tim Peters, The Zen of Python (PEP 20). Type import this in Python to read all nineteen lines.
The try statement in both languages

Same jobs, different names. Python adds an else clause. Java puts that code at the end of the try block.

JobJavaPython
try something that may failtry { … }try:
handle one kind of failurecatch (NumberFormatException e) { … }except ValueError as e:
handle two kinds the same waycatch (NumberFormatException | ArithmeticException e)except (ValueError, ZeroDivisionError) as e:
run only if nothing failed(the end of the try block)else:
always run on the way outfinally { … }finally:
the exception’s messagee.getMessage()str(e)
its type, as texte.getClass().getSimpleName()type(e).__name__
report a failure yourselfthrow new IllegalArgumentException("…");raise ValueError("…")

Handlers are checked top to bottom, and the first match wins. Put the most specific one first.

Order matters

catch (Exception e) above catch (NumberFormatException e) catches everything first. Java will not compile it: exception NumberFormatException has already been caught. Python accepts it, and the second handler never runs.
Exceptions you will meet this week

The exception’s name tells you what happened.

What happenedJavaPython
text is not a whole numberInteger.parseInt("abc") → NumberFormatExceptionint("abc") → ValueError
whole-number division by zero7 / 0 → ArithmeticException7 // 0 → ZeroDivisionError
index past the endArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, IndexOutOfBoundsExceptionIndexError
using an object that is not thereNullPointerExceptionAttributeError on None
Scanner.nextInt() meets a wordInputMismatchException(no Scanner: int(input()) gives ValueError)
reading after the input has endednextLine() → NoSuchElementExceptioninput() → EOFError
file not foundFileNotFoundException, NoSuchFileExceptionFileNotFoundError

The languages disagree on what a number is. Python’s int(" 85 ") ignores the spaces and gives 85. Java’s Integer.parseInt(" 85") throws. Both accept "+7". Neither accepts "3.0". Try these in the first diagram below.

Check first, or try first?

Java code often checks first: while (in.hasNextInt()). Python code often tries and handles the exception (section 3’s Did you know? names this style). Both are fine. Converting typed text with neither is not.

media.alt: A green sign on a lamp post reading “Fire assembly point”, with a pictogram of a family grouped together, against wooded hills and a blue sky
media.lead: Drop everything and go to the assembly point.
media.caption: When the fire alarm sounds, nobody finishes the sentence they were typing: everyone stops and goes to the agreed assembly point. A thrown exception works the same way. The statement that failed stops, the rest of the try block is skipped, and control goes straight to the matching catch or except. Once the handler has dealt with it, the program carries on after the whole try statement, like people going back inside after the all-clear. Where it breaks: a fire drill is rehearsed; an exception reports something that really went wrong.

media.alt: Five round outdoor bins in a row, yellow for paper, silver for aluminium, green for glass, blue for PET bottles and red for general waste, each labelled in several languages
media.lead: One bin for each kind of thing.
media.caption: Each bin takes one kind of rubbish, and its label says which. A specific handler is a labelled bin: catch (NumberFormatException e) or except ValueError takes only failed conversions, so when it runs you know exactly what happened. catch (Exception e) is the red bin on the right, labelled waste: everything fits, including things that belonged somewhere else, and nobody notices. A broad handler hides bugs the same quiet way.

media.title: Invisible Formatting
media.alt: xkcd comic in six panels of a word processor. A user selects the word “not”, clicks Bold, thinks “nah, the bold is too much”, selects it again and clicks Bold off; but the space after “not” stays bold: a hidden bold space. Caption: When editing text, in the back of my mind I always worry that I’m adding invisible formatting that will somehow cause a problem in the distant future.
media.caption: In the first diagram, Java refuses " 5" because of one character you cannot see. When a conversion fails on input that looks right, print the input inside quotes (or with repr in Python) so hidden spaces and line breaks show up.

media.alt: An Ariane 5 rocket standing on its launch pad at night, lit by floodlights, between tall lightning towers
media.text: On 4 June 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket broke up about 40 seconds into its flight. Its guidance software converted a 64-bit floating-point number into a 16-bit signed integer; the value was too big to fit, and the conversion raised an exception (an “Operand Error”) that nothing handled. Other conversions in the same code were protected; this one was not. The back-up guidance computer ran the same software and had already failed in the same way. Pictured: a later Ariane 5 before the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope in 2021.

sections.title: Propagation, checked exceptions and cleanup
concepts: Throw here, handle at the right level

Each method call gets a frame on the call stack, holding its parameters and local variables. The newest frame is on top.

If a method throws and has no matching handler, its frame is abandoned at once. The exception arrives at the line that called it, and the search repeats there. If no frame handles it, main is abandoned too and the program stops. This is propagation (unwinding the stack).

So catch where something useful can happen. parseMark cannot ask the user again, but the input loop in main can. Throw where the problem is found, with a clear message: throw new IllegalArgumentException("mark out of range: " + mark); in Java, raise ValueError(f"mark out of range: {mark}") in Python.

Reading a stack trace

A Java stack trace lists the newest frame first. A Python traceback (“most recent call last”) lists it last. In both, find the first line that names your file.
Cleanup is separate from success

A finally block runs whenever control leaves the try statement: normally, after a handler, while an exception propagates, or through a return. Only stopping the program outright, such as Java’s System.exit, skips it.

So finally running does not mean the work succeeded. Track success separately.

To close a resource, use Java’s try-with-resources, try (BufferedReader in = …) { … }, or Python’s with open(…) as f:. Both close it on every way out.

Never return from finally

A return inside finally replaces the try block’s result, and an exception on its way up vanishes without a trace. Use finally for cleanup only.
Checked or unchecked: Java’s family tree

Java exceptions form one class tree. A handler for a class also catches its subclasses.

java.lang.Throwable and some of its subclasses
Throwable
├── Error                         serious JVM problems: do not catch
│   ├── OutOfMemoryError
│   └── StackOverflowError
└── Exception                     checked, except the RuntimeException branch
    ├── IOException               checked
    │   └── FileNotFoundException
    └── RuntimeException          unchecked
        ├── IllegalArgumentException
        │   └── NumberFormatException
        ├── ArithmeticException
        ├── NullPointerException
        └── IndexOutOfBoundsException

A checked exception is under Exception but not under RuntimeException. The compiler makes you catch it, or declare it with throws, which passes the duty to every caller. Otherwise javac stops with unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown.

Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and below, and Error) carry no such duty.

  • catch (IllegalArgumentException e) also catches its subclass NumberFormatException.
  • throws only declares. It never handles anything.

If a client can reasonably be expected to recover from an exception, make it a checked exception. If a client cannot do anything to recover from the exception, make it an unchecked exception.

The Java Tutorials, “Unchecked Exceptions — The Controversy”
And Python?

Python has a similar tree (BaseException → Exception → ValueError) but no checked exceptions. Say it in the docstring: “Raises ValueError if the mark is outside 0 to 100.”

A bare except catches Ctrl+C

A bare except: also catches KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl+C) and SystemExit. Inside a loop, the program can become impossible to stop. Name the exception, or at the widest write except Exception.
Catch, declare, or let it crash?

The real skill is deciding where each failure belongs:

SituationWhat to doWhy
The user typed a word where a number belongsCatch it there, explain, and ask againOnly the input loop can ask again
A file the user named is missingCatch it where you talk to the user, and name the fileIt is expected. A stack trace is not a message
A helper method cannot decide what to doLet it propagate: throws IOException in Java, a docstring line in PythonIts caller knows the context
A rule is broken: a mark of 120throw / raise, with the bad value in the messageFail where the rule breaks, not three methods later
NullPointerException, IndexError and friendsDo not catch them: fix the codeThese are bugs, not bad input
Something has to be closedtry-with-resources, or withIt closes on every path

catch (Exception e) { } is the programming version of taking the battery out of a smoke alarm because the beeping is annoying.

A Week 9 rule of thumb

visuals.title: Checked or unchecked? Ask the compiler
visuals.intro: Choose how load is declared and what its body does. Nothing runs: this only asks the compiler whether the program is allowed. A checked exception, such as IOException, must be caught or declared with throws. An unchecked one (RuntimeException and its subclasses) need not be. The messages are what javac prints on Ed.

decls.label: … throws IOException
decls.code: static void load(String name) throws IOException {

stmts.py: raise OSError("cannot read " + name) is always allowed. Python has no checked exceptions: nothing is checked before the program runs.

plain.say: IOException is checked. The method neither catches nor declares it, so the compiler refuses the program.

throws.say: Declared, so allowed. The duty moves to the caller: main must catch or declare it too, and here it declares throws IOException.

stmts.py: open(name) may raise FileNotFoundError, but Python never makes you declare or catch it.

plain.say: The FileReader constructor declares throws FileNotFoundException, a checked exception. Calling it brings the same duty as throwing it yourself.

throws.say: FileNotFoundException is a kind of IOException, so throws IOException covers it.

stmts.py: raise ValueError("bad name: " + name) runs; Python treats every exception the same way here.

throws.say: Still allowed. The throws clause is about IOException. An unchecked exception needs no declaration either way.

stmts.py: int(name) may raise ValueError; nothing has to be declared.

plain.say: parseInt can throw NumberFormatException, but it is unchecked, so the compiler asks for nothing. Catching it is still your choice.

throws.say: Allowed. throws IOException neither helps nor hurts an unchecked exception.

sections.title: Tokens, lines and end of input
concepts: Choose a reading contract

First ask how the input is laid out.

  • Tokens: values separated by any whitespace. Line breaks do not matter. Use Scanner.nextInt() in Java or sys.stdin.read().split() in Python.
  • Line records: one record per line, such as Linh,85. Read whole lines, then split each one.
  • Free text: names like Le Linh. A token reader would cut it in two, so read lines.

Scanner skips all whitespace, line breaks included, before each token. So the example below adds three numbers spread over two lines.

hasNextInt() stops at a word, too

while (in.hasNextInt()) also stops at the first non-integer. Input 10 20 x 30 gives 30 and silently leaves x 30 unread. To report stray words, read with next() and convert yourself.
Do not confuse a blank line with EOF

The end-of-input signal (EOF, “end of file”) must differ from every real line, even an empty one.

Read returns…Java readLine()Python readline()
a line"tea" (no line break)"tea " (line break kept)
a blank line""" "
end of inputnull (not a string)""

The Python tutorial: “if f.readline() returns an empty string, the end of the file has been reached, while a blank line is represented by ' '”.

In Python, for line in file: is simpler: it stops at the end by itself. Remove each line’s " " with line.rstrip(" "). Mind the spelling: Java readLine(), Python readline().

The blank-line bug

if not line.strip(): break stops at the first blank line and silently drops every later record (second diagram below). Test for null in Java. In Python, let the for loop end by itself.
Reading methods side by side

in is a BufferedReader, sc a Scanner, f an open Python file.

The nextInt() then nextLine() trap

nextInt() leaves the line break behind, so the next nextLine() returns an empty string. Call nextLine() once to discard it, or read every line and convert with Integer.parseInt. The explained example at the end of this section shows the trap.
Ending the input yourself, and null

At a terminal, you end keyboard input yourself: Ctrl+D at the start of a line on macOS and Linux, or Ctrl+Z then Enter on Windows. A file or test input ends where its text ends.

In Java, test for null before using the line: line.length() on null throws NullPointerException. The condition (line = in.readLine()) != null reads, stores and tests in one step.

I call it my billion-dollar mistake. It was the invention of the null reference in 1965.

C. A. R. Hoare, abstract of Null References: The Billion Dollar Mistake, QCon London 2009 Portrait: Rama, 2011 · CC BY-SA 2.0 fr

Hoare added the null reference to ALGOL W, he wrote, “simply because it was so easy to implement”.

media.alt: A red buffer stop at the end of a railway track beside an empty platform, with a town and hills behind
media.text: Every Python for loop ends with an exception. The loop asks its iterator for the next item again and again; when there are no more, the iterator raises StopIteration, which tells the for loop to stop. You never see it, because the loop handles it. Reading a file line by line ends the same way. Python’s glossary has a name for this style of trying first and handling the exception: EAFP, “easier to ask for forgiveness than permission”.

sections.title: Readers, resource scope and real files
concepts: Read until the reader reports EOF

Java reads text through a chain of readers:

  • A FileReader, or a StringReader for text in memory, supplies characters.
  • A BufferedReader wraps it, reads in large chunks and adds readLine().
  • Files.newBufferedReader(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) builds this chain and names the encoding in one call.

Loop until readLine() returns null. It returns the line “or null if the end of the stream has been reached”. Do not test ready(): it only says whether a read could go ahead without waiting.

The examples read from a StringReader or StringIO so they run in your browser. On Ed, swap in a file reader. The loop stays the same.
File paths and text encoding

A relative path such as data/marks.txt starts from the working directory: the folder the program started in. An IDE may use the project folder, not your source folder. An absolute path (/home/linh/marks.txt, C:\Users\Linh\marks.txt) starts at the top of the file system.

File not found? Print the working directory: System.getProperty("user.dir") or os.getcwd(). A missing file is expected, not a bug. Catch FileNotFoundException or NoSuchFileException (Java), or FileNotFoundError (Python), and name the file.

An encoding says which bytes mean which characters. Always name UTF-8. Java 8’s FileReader and older Pythons use the machine’s default, which varies. Java 18+ and Python 3.15+ default to UTF-8, but naming it keeps names like Nguyễn safe on every version.

Small files, big files

A list of every line is fine for a class list. A loop that reads one line at a time handles a file of any size.
A robust reading loop, step by step

Real files contain mistakes. A good loop reports each one and keeps going:

  1. Open with try-with-resources or with. Report a missing file.
  2. Loop to the end signal, counting lines so messages can say line 4.
  3. Remove the line break. Handle blank lines on purpose: skip or report.
  4. Split the record and check the number of fields.
  5. Convert inside a small try. On failure, report the line number and text, then continue.
  6. Check the range: 120 is a number, but not a mark.
  7. After the loop, print a summary.

The explained example Report every bad record and keep going, at the end of this section, follows these steps in Python.

One bad line must not cost the rest

A try around the whole loop ends it at the first bad record, losing every later one. Put the try inside the loop, around one record.

extras.code:
from io import StringIO

data = StringIO("Linh,85\nAn,abc\n\nMai,120\nBao,49\nVy\n")
total = count = 0
for number, line in enumerate(data, 1):
    line = line.rstrip("\n")
    if not line:
        print(f"line {number}: blank, skipped")
        continue
    parts = line.split(",")
    if len(parts) != 2:
        print(f"line {number}: expected name,mark but got {line!r}")
        continue
    name, text = parts
    try:
        mark = int(text)
    except ValueError:
        print(f"line {number}: {text!r} is not a whole number")
        continue
    if not 0 <= mark <= 100:
        print(f"line {number}: mark {mark} is out of range")
        continue
    total += mark
    count += 1
print(f"{count} good records, average {total / count:.1f}")

questions.q: What does Java throws IOException do?
questions.correct: Declares that the method may propagate that checked exception.
wrong: Catches every IOException automatically and then resumes the failed file read.
Creates a new IOException object on every call even when the operation succeeds.
Guarantees that the caller will always recover without writing any handling code.
questions.why: throws is a declaration, while try/catch performs handling.

questions.q: Which is the correct EOF condition for BufferedReader.readLine()?
wrong: The returned string is empty, because a blank line can never occur in a text file.
The ready() method returns true, because readiness always means no more text exists.
The last line lacks a newline, because a final unterminated line must be discarded.
questions.why: An empty string represents a blank line. readLine also returns a final line without a trailing newline.

questions.q: Why keep the try block narrow around parsing?
questions.correct: So the handler covers the expected failure without hiding unrelated bugs.
wrong: So Java treats every checked exception as unchecked and stops checking the method.
So the program never needs to validate the range of a successfully parsed value.
So Python is forced to choose the same exception type for every possible error.
questions.why: A specific handler and a small try block document exactly what can be recovered from.

questions.q: What does a context manager or try-with-resources contribute?
questions.correct: It closes the managed resource when its scope exits.
wrong: It proves that file content is valid and every row contains the expected number of columns.
It prevents every possible exception from occurring anywhere inside the managed block.
It creates the missing input file automatically before a read-mode open is attempted.
questions.why: Resource lifetime management does not validate content or guarantee I/O success.

misc.title: Where exceptions came from
misc.html:
Not examinable. try, catch and throws were argued over for decades. Knowing the argument makes the rules feel less arbitrary.

1975

Exceptions get a notation

John B. Goodenough publishes Exception Handling: Issues and a Proposed Notation (Communications of the ACM 18(12)), an early systematic look at reporting and handling failures.

1979

CLU: a failure is part of the method’s contract

Barbara Liskov and Alan Snyder describe CLU’s exceptions in Exception Handling in CLU (IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering). Liskov later won the 2008 Turing Award.

1980

Hoare’s warning

In his Turing Award lecture, Tony Hoare criticises the new Ada language’s many features, “some of them, like exception handling, even dangerous” (quoted below).

1996

Java makes some exceptions checked

Java 1.0 ships with the rule from section 2: an IOException must be caught or declared, a RuntimeException need not be. That year, an unhandled conversion exception destroys the first Ariane 5 (see M2).

2003

C# leaves them out

In The Trouble with Checked Exceptions, C#’s lead designer Anders Hejlsberg explains why C# has none: “I see two big issues with checked exceptions: scalability and versionability.”

2005–06

Python gets the with statement

PEP 343, by Guido van Rossum and Alyssa Coghlan, adds the with statement (Python 2.5). Closing a file no longer needs a hand-written finally.

2011

Java SE 7: try-with-resources and multi-catch

try-with-resources closes anything AutoCloseable. One catch can name several types with |.

Today

The debate goes on

Kotlin, a newer Java-platform language, “treats all exceptions as unchecked” (Kotlin documentation). Java still checks them.

…supposedly achieved by a plethora of features and notational conventions, many of them unnecessary and some of them, like exception handling, even dangerous.

C. A. R. Hoare, The Emperor’s Old Clothes, 1980 ACM Turing Award Lecture, on Ada Portrait: Rama, 2011 · CC BY-SA 2.0 fr

Hoare lost: exception handling is now in almost every mainstream language. But his worry runs through this week. A handler is a hidden jump, and a careless one hides failures. Use few handlers, specific types and small try blocks.

misc.title: Ariane 501: the handler that made it worse
misc.html:
Section 1’s Did you know? gives the short version. The details are a lesson in exception handling, not arithmetic. All quotes are from the report of the Ariane 501 Inquiry Board (July 1996; ESA’s scan).

What happened

  • The inertial reference system (SRI) was “practically the same as that of an SRI which is presently used on Ariane 4, particularly as regards the software”.
  • An alignment function kept running after launch, although “As soon as the launcher lifts off, this function serves no purpose.”
  • It produced “an unexpected high value of an internal alignment function result called BH, Horizontal Bias”. Converting it from a 64-bit floating-point number to a 16-bit signed integer failed with an Operand Error.
  • Seven variables were found at risk of such an error. Four were protected. Three were not, because “they were either physically limited or that there was a large margin of safety”. The board was told not all conversions were protected because of an 80% maximum workload target for the computer.

The handler made it worse

There was a response. The specification said “the failure should be indicated on the databus” and “the SRI processor should be shut down”. That suits a random hardware fault, where a back-up unit takes over: the mechanisms “are designed for a random hardware failure which can quite rationally be handled by a backup system”. But the back-up SRI ran the same software on the same data. It had already shut down “during the previous data cycle (72 milliseconds period) for the same reason”. The active unit followed about 0.05 seconds later.

“It was the decision to cease the processor operation which finally proved fatal.”
Ariane 501 Inquiry Board report, 1996

The board’s summary: “The exception was detected, but inappropriately handled because the view had been taken that software should be considered correct until it is shown to be at fault.”

What it means for a Week 9 program

In the reportIn your code
Three conversions were left unprotectedEvery conversion of outside data (a user, a file) needs a check or a handler
The handler shut the unit down, whatever the causeA handler should fit its failure. One response for everything is a broad catch
The back-up ran the same code and failed the same wayRetrying the same thing with the same input gives the same exception
The failing function served no purpose after lift-offUnneeded code can still fail. Delete what you do not use
